title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
For the Department of Development & Education of Youth in Diverse Societies
Course coordinators: Robert Bagheri, Pablo Mosteiro, Laurence Frank, Ozgur Togay (Department of Methodology, Statistics and Data Science)
Duration: 1 hour
This tutorial was drafted with assistance from GPT-5.6-Sol. All examples below are AI generated.


By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

Use UU AI-Chat and choose an appropriate way to organise your work using chats, prompts, personas, projects, and groups.
Use AI assistants for common research tasks, including:

extracting relevant information from text,
coding, classifying, or annotating text,
summarising or comparing research material.

Turn useful one-off prompts into more reusable research workflows.
Critically evaluate AI-generated output and recognise important limitations.





For this tutorial, we will use UU AI-Chat, Utrecht University’s generative AI environment. Sign in with your UU account and start a new chat.
UU AI-Chat provides access to several language models and supports files such as PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and text files. It also includes tools for web search, data analysis, code execution, image generation, and other tasks.


You do not need to use every feature in this tutorial. The main options in the left sidebar serve different purposes:







Feature
Useful when…




Chat
You want to ask a question, analyse a file, or carry out a one-off task.


Personas
You want a reusable AI assistant with a consistent role, instructions, or source material for a recurring task.


Projects
You want to keep related chats, files, instructions, and other material together for an ongoing research task.


Groups
You want to share reusable resources such as prompts or personas and collaborate with other UU AI-Chat users.


Prompts
You want to save an instruction that you expect to use again instead of rewriting it each time.




The chat screen also contains ready-made prompts for common tasks. For example, under Research you will find prompts for developing hypotheses or engaging with research literature. Treat these as starting points: inspect what the prompt asks the model to do, adapt it to your research question, and evaluate the result critically.



For the exercises below, the default model is usually sufficient. You can browse or switch models using the model button in the bottom-right corner of the chat.
Different models may vary in capability, speed, and computing requirements. UU AI-Chat indicates relative computing or energy use in the model selector. Use a more demanding model when the task benefits from it, rather than automatically choosing the largest option.



When an exercise uses research material, you can either paste the relevant text into the chat or upload the source file. When working from an uploaded document, tell the model clearly which document it should use and what information it should base its answer on.
Throughout the tutorial, remember that the model’s output can be incomplete or incorrect even when it is based on an uploaded source.







Scenario: You have a short classroom observation about multilingual pupils’ participation during a collaborative learning activity.
Copy this prompt to your AI chat:
Extract the key information from the classroom observation below.

Identify:
1. Observable instances of participation and language use.
2. Teacher or peer actions that may be relevant to participation.
3. Ambiguities or missing context.

Support your points with details from the observation. Separate observation from interpretation, and do not infer traits or motives that are not directly supported.

Observation:
"During a small-group science task, the teacher asked pupils to discuss why one object floated and another sank. Lina first discussed her idea quietly in Arabic with Samira. Samira then summarized part of their discussion in Dutch. The teacher told the group that they could use any language while working out the problem, but that the group should present its final explanation in Dutch. Later, Lina raised her hand when the teacher asked groups to report back, but another pupil from the group answered after the teacher called on the group. At the end of the lesson, Lina completed the written explanation independently."
Task: Use the BRAVE(R) framework to analyze the prompt, then use the FACTS framework to analyze the response. Discuss your evaluation with a classmate.
Note: LLMs can also help you build and refine prompts.



Did the model distinguish observation from interpretation?
Did it support its claims with details from the excerpt?
What would you need to know before drawing broader conclusions about participation or inclusion?

If this is a task you expect to repeat, consider saving the instructions as a Prompt. A saved prompt is useful when the instructions stay mostly the same but the input changes.





Scenario: You want to explore caregivers’ needs, challenges, strategies, and cultural factors related to toilet training autistic children using two synthetic focus-group excerpts.
Copy this prompt to your AI chat:
Analyze the two synthetic focus-group excerpts below in relation to this research question:

What are the needs, challenges, strategies, and cultural factors that shape toilet-training practices for autistic children in these two focus groups?

Identify evidence for each of the four themes. Keep the two focus groups distinguishable, support interpretations with speaker IDs or short excerpts, and note ambiguity rather than filling in missing information.

These texts are fictional training materials. Do not treat them as representative of caregivers, autistic children, or toilet-training practices in Malaysia or Morocco.

Focus group 1 — Malaysia:

Moderator: What has been most difficult about toilet training for your child?

M1: "My son does not always tell us that he needs the toilet. Sometimes we notice from his behaviour, but by then it can be too late. I would like clearer guidance on how to recognise his signals without pushing him too much."

M2: "For my daughter, the bathroom itself can be difficult. She dislikes the sound of the flush and gets upset when the floor is wet. At home we let her leave before we flush, and we use the same picture sequence every time. Public toilets are harder because we cannot control the noise."

M3: "The family also has different ideas about when a child should already be toilet trained. Some relatives compare my son with his cousins and ask why he still needs help. That creates pressure. His grandmother wanted us to put him on the toilet at fixed times very often, but he became resistant. We eventually agreed on a routine that gives him more time."

Moderator: Are there differences between places where your child uses the toilet?

M4: "Yes. At home we have a sitting toilet, but at my parents' house there is a squat toilet. My daughter was confused by the change. We used pictures and a small foot support to practise the different steps before visiting them."

M1: "Consistency between home and school helps us most. When the teacher started using the same words and picture card that we use at home, my son understood the routine more quickly."

M3: "I would also like information that everyone in the family can use. Some guidance we received was in English and was too detailed for my mother. A short version with pictures and simple Malay would make it easier for us to follow the same approach."

Moderator: What strategies have been helpful?

M2: "A predictable routine, pictures, and not making an accident into a big event. If she is distressed, we stop and try later. The biggest improvement came when home and school agreed on the same steps."


Focus group 2 — Morocco:

Moderator: Chno huwa akbar taḥaddi f toilet training? [What is the biggest challenge in toilet training?]

R1: "Bnti katjbed yeddi ila bghat chi haja, walakin ma kanʿrafch dima wash katqsed toilette." [My daughter takes my hand when she wants something, but I do not always know whether she means the toilet.] "I need practical ways to help her communicate the need earlier without expecting spoken words."

R2: "Mon fils est très sensible au bruit dans les toilettes." [My son is very sensitive to noise in bathrooms.] "The echo and the hand dryer in some places frighten him. We first practised when the bathroom was quiet and used a simple visual sequence. Now he manages at home, but unfamiliar toilets are still difficult."

R3: "Several relatives are involved because we live close to my parents and they help with care. That can be useful, but everyone gives different advice. Waḥed kaygol khassek tkon ṣarem, waḥed kaygol khallih b raḥto." [One person says you should be strict, another says leave him at his own pace.] "We found it works better when everybody follows the same routine and accidents do not become a conflict."

Moderator: Are there household or family practices that affect the routine?

R4: "In our home we normally use water for cleaning after the toilet. My son disliked the sensation at first, so we introduced it gradually and let him control when the water touched his skin. At school the routine is different, so moving between the two settings still takes preparation."

R1: "Some information we received was in French. Moi, je peux le lire, mais ma mère préfère l'arabe, et à la maison on parle surtout darija." [I can read it, but my mother prefers Arabic, and at home we mostly speak Darija.] "Pictures and short instructions that all caregivers understand would make it easier to stay consistent."

Moderator: What has helped most?

R2: "La coordination avec l'enseignante." [Coordination with the teacher.] "We agreed on the same cue and roughly the same sequence of steps. We also stopped treating speed as the main goal. When he became anxious, we went back to an easier step and tried again later."

R3: "For us it was important that relatives understood that the same approach does not work for every child. Once we agreed on a routine and stopped comparing him with other children, there was less tension around toileting."
Task: Before sending the prompt, adapt it using the BRAVE(R) framework. For example, decide how you want the four themes organized and what kind of evidence the response should provide.
If useful, create a Project for the exercise and a simple Persona with reusable qualitative-analysis instructions, such as staying close to the supplied texts and distinguishing evidence from interpretation.
Then run the prompt and use the FACTS framework to evaluate the response.
Data protection: These excerpts are synthetic. Before using real focus-group, interview, or other research data that may contain personal or sensitive information with GenAI, check the applicable requirements with the relevant privacy or data-protection contact. Do not assume that using UU AI-Chat alone is sufficient clearance.
Note: You can include a codebook in the prompt. Clear definitions, decision rules, and output formats can make repeated classifications more consistent.



Did the model distinguish the four themes and support them with evidence from the texts?
Did it preserve differences between the two focus groups rather than generalising from them?
Which instructions would be useful to save in a reusable Persona, and which are specific to this research question?

For a recurring task with stable instructions to the AI assistant, a Persona may be more useful than repeatedly pasting the full setup into a new chat.





Scenario: You need to quickly assess whether a paper is relevant to research on children’s development, learning, participation, or educational contexts.
Choose an abstract, article excerpt, or paper that you would like to work with. You can either paste the relevant text into the prompt or upload the document directly.
If the prompt contains [INSERT TEXT HERE]:

replace it with your chosen text; or
if you uploaded a document, replace it with an instruction such as Use the uploaded document as the source.

Summarize the research abstract below for a researcher deciding whether the study is relevant to their work on child or youth development and education.

Provide:
1. The research question, population, and setting.
2. The study design and main concepts or outcomes.
3. The main findings.
4. Any stated limitations or boundary conditions.
5. What would require reading the full paper.

If relevant, note how diversity, inequality, social context, or participation is addressed. Use only information from the abstract and mark uncertainty clearly.

Abstract:
[INSERT ABSTRACT TEXT HERE]
Task: Use the FACTS framework to analyze the response. Discuss your evaluation with a classmate.



Did the model stay within what the abstract actually supports?
Did it avoid overstating causality or generalisability?
Would the summary help you decide whether to read the full paper?

Compare your result with one of the ready-made Research prompts in UU AI-Chat. What assumptions does the built-in prompt make? What would you add or change for your own research question?
If you are working on different parts of the same research project, consider creating a Project. Chats within a Project can share context, so you can use separate chats for the literature review, methods, analysis, or other parts while keeping them connected.






A useful prompt is not always the final form of an AI-assisted workflow. After completing the examples above, choose one prompt or task that you found useful and decide how you would reuse it:

Save it as a Prompt if you mainly want to reuse the same instruction.
Create a Persona if the AI should consistently follow a particular role, method, codebook, or set of instructions.
Create a Project if the work involves multiple related chats, files, or recurring context.
Use a Group if prompts or personas should be shared with collaborators.

Task: Pick one example from this tutorial and explain which option you would use for a real research workflow and why.
The purpose is not to use the most features. Use the simplest setup that keeps the task clear, reproducible, and easy to review.






Task: Ask the model:
Find three peer-reviewed empirical studies published in 2026 about digital technologies and social participation, learning, or development among children or adolescents. For each study, provide the title, authors, journal, DOI, study population, and one-sentence main finding.
Verify the references and findings using reliable external sources such as journal websites, Crossref, Google Scholar, or another academic database.



Do the publications and bibliographic details exist as given?
Do the reported findings match the original sources?
What would make this literature-search workflow more reliable?






Task: Compare responses to these two prompts:
Prompt A:
Explain why multilingual children participate less in classroom discussions than monolingual children.
Prompt B:
Discuss factors that may be associated with variation in classroom participation among multilingual and monolingual children. Do not assume that a group difference exists. Distinguish empirical evidence from possible explanations.
Compare how the framing affects what the model treats as established.



Did Prompt A encourage the model to accept an unsupported assumption?
Did either response overgeneralise or rely on stereotypes?
How could you phrase your own research questions to reduce leading assumptions?







Create your own checklist:

I will verify AI-generated facts and interpretations.
I will check citations and source claims against the original sources.
I will follow UU rules for confidential, sensitive, and personal data.
I will disclose AI assistance when required.
I will keep human oversight over important research decisions.
I will use saved prompts, personas, or projects only when they make my workflow clearer or more reproducible.
I will choose a level of model capability and computing use appropriate for the task.




For tasks that need to be applied systematically to large amounts of data, API-based workflows may be more appropriate. The Department of Methodology, Statistics and Data Science provides consultation on AI use in research: Consultation Data Science / AI
More information about the university platform is available on the UU AI platforms page.



Use BRAVE(R) when formulating or improving a prompt. Use FACTS when evaluating an AI-generated response.









B: Boundaries
Set limits on the format, length, or any other constraints.


R: Role
Identify the role or perspective you want the AI tool to take.


A: Audience
Specify who the output is intended for to determine the appropriate tone and style.


V: Variables
Highlight key details, variables, or points that should be included in the response.


E: Expectations
Clearly state what you expect the AI to accomplish, including the intended outcome and purpose.


R: Refine
Provide feedback to improve the output and guide future interactions.















F: Focus
Focus on the AI’s response by breaking it down into its main points and arguments.


A: Authenticate
Authenticate the AI’s output by verifying it against current research and empirical data.


C: Critique
Critique the response’s accuracy, relevance, and depth in the context of the topic.


T: Think
Think about the response from different perspectives and consider its potential impact.


S: Scrutinise
Scrutinise the AI’s conclusions by critically questioning them and exploring alternative hypotheses or interpretations.











View the research prompt

LLMs are increasingly used for data annotation because they can make large-scale coding faster and cheaper. Performance still depends on the task, but recent work has found that LLMs can match or outperform human annotators on some social-science text classification tasks (Törnberg, 2024).1
The example below comes from Togay et al. (2026), which used LLMs to identify the political target and stance in Reddit comments across 138 predefined political targets plus an open-ended category. The best-performing models were comparable to highly trained human annotators.2
This is deliberately much longer than the tutorial prompts above. Research annotation prompts can function like codebooks: they define labels, edge cases, output formats, and examples so that the same rules can be applied consistently across many observations. This prompt was also designed for an earlier generation of models; repeated emphasis such as **...** was used to reinforce important instructions and is generally not necessary with newer models.
You will be provided with a Reddit comment and the title of the submission under which it was posted.

Your task is to identify the **target** and the **stance** expressed toward it in the Comment, using the predefined list of political targets at the end.

Only classify stances related to a target from the list. If the Comment refers to a similar target with different wording, select the exact matching entry from the list.  
**Do not rename, paraphrase, or invent new target names.**  
- If the post refers to a target not on the list, label it **"Other"**.  
- If no political target is mentioned, label it **"None"**.  

Use the Submission **only** to resolve ambiguity (e.g., resolving pronouns or vague references). **Do not infer stance from the Submission.**

---

## Classification Steps

1. **Identify the Political Target**  
   - Choose a target from the predefined list at the end.  
   - If the post refers to a target not on the list, label it **"Other"**.  
   - If no target is mentioned, label it **"None"** and skip stance classification.

2. **Determine the Stance** (only if a target is identified)  
   - **Positive**: clear support or praise  
   - **Neutral**: mention without a clear stance  
   - **Negative**: criticism or disapproval
   - **None**: no stance can be identified

3. **Return the classification**

---

## Output Format

Your response must be a JSON object with the following fields:
- "target" (string): The identified political target, from the list of Predefined Targets.
- "stance" (string): The determined stance. Must be one of: "Positive", "Neutral", "Negative", or "None".
- "confidence" (float): A confidence score between 0.0 and 1.0 (inclusive) representing how certain the model is about its classification.

Example JSON output if a target and stance are identified:
```json
(
  "target": "Donald Trump",
  "stance": "Positive",
  "confidence": 0.95
)

## Examples

# Example 1
Input:
    Submission Title: New York Primary Results Megathread   
    Comment: Didn't Sanders vote for that crime bill too? Has he evolved on that position or does he still support it?  
Output:
```json
(
  "target": "Bernie Sanders",
  "stance": "Neutral",
  "confidence": 0.8
)

# Example 2
Input:
    Submission Title: Flat-tax in the U.S. - a good idea?   
    Comment: I'd say it's a good thing, but the reason for existing tax breaks is to encourage people to live in a way that is good for society; get educated, own property, have kids, etc.    
Output:
```json
(
  "target": "Tax cuts (general)",
  "stance": "Positive",
  "confidence": 0.90
)

# Example 3
Input:
    Submission Title: Is drug legalization/decriminalization sound policy? 
    Comment: "Treating drug abuse as a medical problem instead of a criminal problem has been successful in European countries and has been a conclusion by various studies.
     
     (let's make the AutoMod happy: )
     
     https://www.drugabuse.gov/about-nida/noras-blog/2014/03/unodc-recommends-treating-addiction-health-not-legal-issue
     
     https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2681083/" 
Output:
```json
(
  "target": "War on Drugs",
  "stance": "Negative",
  "confidence": 0.90
)

# Example 4
Input:
    Submission Title: What are the benefits and costs of the federal hiring freeze? 
    Comment: I will note you didn't call out the dude who cited a government agency to show government agency hiring shouldn't be frozen.   
Output:
(
  "target": "None",
  "stance": "None",
  "confidence": 1.0
)

---

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

Use UU AI-Chat and choose an appropriate way to organise your work using chats, prompts, personas, projects, and groups.
Use AI assistants for common research tasks, including:

extracting relevant information from text,
coding, classifying, or annotating text,
summarising or comparing research material.

Turn useful one-off prompts into more reusable research workflows.
Critically evaluate AI-generated output and recognise important limitations.

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
For this tutorial, we will use UU AI-Chat, Utrecht University’s generative AI environment. Sign in with your UU account and start a new chat.
UU AI-Chat provides access to several language models and supports files such as PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and text files. It also includes tools for web search, data analysis, code execution, image generation, and other tasks.


You do not need to use every feature in this tutorial. The main options in the left sidebar serve different purposes:







Feature
Useful when…




Chat
You want to ask a question, analyse a file, or carry out a one-off task.


Personas
You want a reusable AI assistant with a consistent role, instructions, or source material for a recurring task.


Projects
You want to keep related chats, files, instructions, and other material together for an ongoing research task.


Groups
You want to share reusable resources such as prompts or personas and collaborate with other UU AI-Chat users.


Prompts
You want to save an instruction that you expect to use again instead of rewriting it each time.




The chat screen also contains ready-made prompts for common tasks. For example, under Research you will find prompts for developing hypotheses or engaging with research literature. Treat these as starting points: inspect what the prompt asks the model to do, adapt it to your research question, and evaluate the result critically.



For the exercises below, the default model is usually sufficient. You can browse or switch models using the model button in the bottom-right corner of the chat.
Different models may vary in capability, speed, and computing requirements. UU AI-Chat indicates relative computing or energy use in the model selector. Use a more demanding model when the task benefits from it, rather than automatically choosing the largest option.



When an exercise uses research material, you can either paste the relevant text into the chat or upload the source file. When working from an uploaded document, tell the model clearly which document it should use and what information it should base its answer on.
Throughout the tutorial, remember that the model’s output can be incomplete or incorrect even when it is based on an uploaded source.

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
Scenario: You have a short classroom observation about multilingual pupils’ participation during a collaborative learning activity.
Copy this prompt to your AI chat:
Extract the key information from the classroom observation below.

Identify:
1. Observable instances of participation and language use.
2. Teacher or peer actions that may be relevant to participation.
3. Ambiguities or missing context.

Support your points with details from the observation. Separate observation from interpretation, and do not infer traits or motives that are not directly supported.

Observation:
"During a small-group science task, the teacher asked pupils to discuss why one object floated and another sank. Lina first discussed her idea quietly in Arabic with Samira. Samira then summarized part of their discussion in Dutch. The teacher told the group that they could use any language while working out the problem, but that the group should present its final explanation in Dutch. Later, Lina raised her hand when the teacher asked groups to report back, but another pupil from the group answered after the teacher called on the group. At the end of the lesson, Lina completed the written explanation independently."
Task: Use the BRAVE(R) framework to analyze the prompt, then use the FACTS framework to analyze the response. Discuss your evaluation with a classmate.
Note: LLMs can also help you build and refine prompts.



Did the model distinguish observation from interpretation?
Did it support its claims with details from the excerpt?
What would you need to know before drawing broader conclusions about participation or inclusion?

If this is a task you expect to repeat, consider saving the instructions as a Prompt. A saved prompt is useful when the instructions stay mostly the same but the input changes.





Scenario: You want to explore caregivers’ needs, challenges, strategies, and cultural factors related to toilet training autistic children using two synthetic focus-group excerpts.
Copy this prompt to your AI chat:
Analyze the two synthetic focus-group excerpts below in relation to this research question:

What are the needs, challenges, strategies, and cultural factors that shape toilet-training practices for autistic children in these two focus groups?

Identify evidence for each of the four themes. Keep the two focus groups distinguishable, support interpretations with speaker IDs or short excerpts, and note ambiguity rather than filling in missing information.

These texts are fictional training materials. Do not treat them as representative of caregivers, autistic children, or toilet-training practices in Malaysia or Morocco.

Focus group 1 — Malaysia:

Moderator: What has been most difficult about toilet training for your child?

M1: "My son does not always tell us that he needs the toilet. Sometimes we notice from his behaviour, but by then it can be too late. I would like clearer guidance on how to recognise his signals without pushing him too much."

M2: "For my daughter, the bathroom itself can be difficult. She dislikes the sound of the flush and gets upset when the floor is wet. At home we let her leave before we flush, and we use the same picture sequence every time. Public toilets are harder because we cannot control the noise."

M3: "The family also has different ideas about when a child should already be toilet trained. Some relatives compare my son with his cousins and ask why he still needs help. That creates pressure. His grandmother wanted us to put him on the toilet at fixed times very often, but he became resistant. We eventually agreed on a routine that gives him more time."

Moderator: Are there differences between places where your child uses the toilet?

M4: "Yes. At home we have a sitting toilet, but at my parents' house there is a squat toilet. My daughter was confused by the change. We used pictures and a small foot support to practise the different steps before visiting them."

M1: "Consistency between home and school helps us most. When the teacher started using the same words and picture card that we use at home, my son understood the routine more quickly."

M3: "I would also like information that everyone in the family can use. Some guidance we received was in English and was too detailed for my mother. A short version with pictures and simple Malay would make it easier for us to follow the same approach."

Moderator: What strategies have been helpful?

M2: "A predictable routine, pictures, and not making an accident into a big event. If she is distressed, we stop and try later. The biggest improvement came when home and school agreed on the same steps."


Focus group 2 — Morocco:

Moderator: Chno huwa akbar taḥaddi f toilet training? [What is the biggest challenge in toilet training?]

R1: "Bnti katjbed yeddi ila bghat chi haja, walakin ma kanʿrafch dima wash katqsed toilette." [My daughter takes my hand when she wants something, but I do not always know whether she means the toilet.] "I need practical ways to help her communicate the need earlier without expecting spoken words."

R2: "Mon fils est très sensible au bruit dans les toilettes." [My son is very sensitive to noise in bathrooms.] "The echo and the hand dryer in some places frighten him. We first practised when the bathroom was quiet and used a simple visual sequence. Now he manages at home, but unfamiliar toilets are still difficult."

R3: "Several relatives are involved because we live close to my parents and they help with care. That can be useful, but everyone gives different advice. Waḥed kaygol khassek tkon ṣarem, waḥed kaygol khallih b raḥto." [One person says you should be strict, another says leave him at his own pace.] "We found it works better when everybody follows the same routine and accidents do not become a conflict."

Moderator: Are there household or family practices that affect the routine?

R4: "In our home we normally use water for cleaning after the toilet. My son disliked the sensation at first, so we introduced it gradually and let him control when the water touched his skin. At school the routine is different, so moving between the two settings still takes preparation."

R1: "Some information we received was in French. Moi, je peux le lire, mais ma mère préfère l'arabe, et à la maison on parle surtout darija." [I can read it, but my mother prefers Arabic, and at home we mostly speak Darija.] "Pictures and short instructions that all caregivers understand would make it easier to stay consistent."

Moderator: What has helped most?

R2: "La coordination avec l'enseignante." [Coordination with the teacher.] "We agreed on the same cue and roughly the same sequence of steps. We also stopped treating speed as the main goal. When he became anxious, we went back to an easier step and tried again later."

R3: "For us it was important that relatives understood that the same approach does not work for every child. Once we agreed on a routine and stopped comparing him with other children, there was less tension around toileting."
Task: Before sending the prompt, adapt it using the BRAVE(R) framework. For example, decide how you want the four themes organized and what kind of evidence the response should provide.
If useful, create a Project for the exercise and a simple Persona with reusable qualitative-analysis instructions, such as staying close to the supplied texts and distinguishing evidence from interpretation.
Then run the prompt and use the FACTS framework to evaluate the response.
Data protection: These excerpts are synthetic. Before using real focus-group, interview, or other research data that may contain personal or sensitive information with GenAI, check the applicable requirements with the relevant privacy or data-protection contact. Do not assume that using UU AI-Chat alone is sufficient clearance.
Note: You can include a codebook in the prompt. Clear definitions, decision rules, and output formats can make repeated classifications more consistent.



Did the model distinguish the four themes and support them with evidence from the texts?
Did it preserve differences between the two focus groups rather than generalising from them?
Which instructions would be useful to save in a reusable Persona, and which are specific to this research question?

For a recurring task with stable instructions to the AI assistant, a Persona may be more useful than repeatedly pasting the full setup into a new chat.





Scenario: You need to quickly assess whether a paper is relevant to research on children’s development, learning, participation, or educational contexts.
Choose an abstract, article excerpt, or paper that you would like to work with. You can either paste the relevant text into the prompt or upload the document directly.
If the prompt contains [INSERT TEXT HERE]:

replace it with your chosen text; or
if you uploaded a document, replace it with an instruction such as Use the uploaded document as the source.

Summarize the research abstract below for a researcher deciding whether the study is relevant to their work on child or youth development and education.

Provide:
1. The research question, population, and setting.
2. The study design and main concepts or outcomes.
3. The main findings.
4. Any stated limitations or boundary conditions.
5. What would require reading the full paper.

If relevant, note how diversity, inequality, social context, or participation is addressed. Use only information from the abstract and mark uncertainty clearly.

Abstract:
[INSERT ABSTRACT TEXT HERE]
Task: Use the FACTS framework to analyze the response. Discuss your evaluation with a classmate.



Did the model stay within what the abstract actually supports?
Did it avoid overstating causality or generalisability?
Would the summary help you decide whether to read the full paper?

Compare your result with one of the ready-made Research prompts in UU AI-Chat. What assumptions does the built-in prompt make? What would you add or change for your own research question?
If you are working on different parts of the same research project, consider creating a Project. Chats within a Project can share context, so you can use separate chats for the literature review, methods, analysis, or other parts while keeping them connected.

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
A useful prompt is not always the final form of an AI-assisted workflow. After completing the examples above, choose one prompt or task that you found useful and decide how you would reuse it:

Save it as a Prompt if you mainly want to reuse the same instruction.
Create a Persona if the AI should consistently follow a particular role, method, codebook, or set of instructions.
Create a Project if the work involves multiple related chats, files, or recurring context.
Use a Group if prompts or personas should be shared with collaborators.

Task: Pick one example from this tutorial and explain which option you would use for a real research workflow and why.
The purpose is not to use the most features. Use the simplest setup that keeps the task clear, reproducible, and easy to review.

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
Task: Ask the model:
Find three peer-reviewed empirical studies published in 2026 about digital technologies and social participation, learning, or development among children or adolescents. For each study, provide the title, authors, journal, DOI, study population, and one-sentence main finding.
Verify the references and findings using reliable external sources such as journal websites, Crossref, Google Scholar, or another academic database.



Do the publications and bibliographic details exist as given?
Do the reported findings match the original sources?
What would make this literature-search workflow more reliable?






Task: Compare responses to these two prompts:
Prompt A:
Explain why multilingual children participate less in classroom discussions than monolingual children.
Prompt B:
Discuss factors that may be associated with variation in classroom participation among multilingual and monolingual children. Do not assume that a group difference exists. Distinguish empirical evidence from possible explanations.
Compare how the framing affects what the model treats as established.



Did Prompt A encourage the model to accept an unsupported assumption?
Did either response overgeneralise or rely on stereotypes?
How could you phrase your own research questions to reduce leading assumptions?

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
Create your own checklist:

I will verify AI-generated facts and interpretations.
I will check citations and source claims against the original sources.
I will follow UU rules for confidential, sensitive, and personal data.
I will disclose AI assistance when required.
I will keep human oversight over important research decisions.
I will use saved prompts, personas, or projects only when they make my workflow clearer or more reproducible.
I will choose a level of model capability and computing use appropriate for the task.

title: Tutorial: How to handle LLMs in your research
text:
Use BRAVE(R) when formulating or improving a prompt. Use FACTS when evaluating an AI-generated response.









B: Boundaries
Set limits on the format, length, or any other constraints.


R: Role
Identify the role or perspective you want the AI tool to take.


A: Audience
Specify who the output is intended for to determine the appropriate tone and style.


V: Variables
Highlight key details, variables, or points that should be included in the response.


E: Expectations
Clearly state what you expect the AI to accomplish, including the intended outcome and purpose.


R: Refine
Provide feedback to improve the output and guide future interactions.















F: Focus
Focus on the AI’s response by breaking it down into its main points and arguments.


A: Authenticate
Authenticate the AI’s output by verifying it against current research and empirical data.


C: Critique
Critique the response’s accuracy, relevance, and depth in the context of the topic.


T: Think
Think about the response from different perspectives and consider its potential impact.


S: Scrutinise
Scrutinise the AI’s conclusions by critically questioning them and exploring alternative hypotheses or interpretations.

text: For this tutorial AI (UU AI-Chat, model gpt-5.1) was used to improve the English grammar and style.

title: Using AI to support coding in R
section: A BRAVE(R) prompt to optimise and annotate the R code
text:
A BRAVE(R) prompt to optimise and annotate the R code
In this exercise, you will use AI as a tutor to explain where and how your R code can be optimised and how it could be better annotated. You will use the BRAVE(R) framework to write a focused prompt. The BRAVE(R) components are: Boundaries, Role, Audience, Variables, Expectations, (Refine).
In UU AI-Chat, you can choose the model you want to work with (see the bottom-right corner of the input window). For coding tasks, the model gpt-5.1 is recommended. Activate this model before you start writing your prompt.
You will work with a Markdown file containing R code from a research project completed at DEEDS (see the file CodeExample.md). Please note that UU AI-Chat currently does not allow uploading R Markdown files (extension .Rmd). It can, however, read Markdown files (extension .md). If your code is currently in an R Markdown file, you can do the following:
In RStudio:

Go to File → New File → Markdown File (instead of “R Markdown File”).
Copy and paste the R code from your .Rmd file into this new .md file.
Save the Markdown file and upload it to UU AI-Chat.

Your request to the AI will consist of two tasks:

Optimise the code: identify where the code can be improved (e.g. clarity, efficiency, readability, reproducibility).
Annotate the improved code: add or improve comments and explanations in the code.

It is best to start with the optimisation task and only then ask for annotation of the improved code, rather than combining everything in a single prompt. This helps to avoid overloading the prompt and keeps the task clear and manageable.

A BRAVE(R) prompt for step 1: code optimisation
Below is an example of how you might formulate your prompt using the BRAVE(R) framework:
Read the R code in the attached Markdown (.md) document and make suggestions for improving clarity, efficiency, and reproducibility (E-Expectations). For this task, you are an expert in R programming for statistical analysis and you will take on the role of an R coding tutor (R – Role). Your explanations should suit a researcher who can write basic R but has limited experience in writing optimised, well-annotated code (A – Audience). First, briefly summarise what the script as a whole does. Next, indicate for which line(s) or code chunk(s) you see possibilities to improve or simplify the code, and explain why each suggested change would be an improvement (V – Variables). Keep your feedback concise: one or two sentences per line or chunk, and do not provide rewritten code at this stage (B – Boundaries).
Question 1: Use the FACTS framework to critically evaluate the AI’s suggestions for code optimisation:

F – Focus: What are the main points and claims the AI makes about your code?
A – Authenticate: Choose one or two specific suggestions. How could you verify whether these suggestions are correct (e.g. R documentation, reproducible tests, consulting a colleague)?
C – Critique: Are there suggestions that are inaccurate, irrelevant, or not useful in your context? Explain why.
T – Think: How might these suggestions affect your analysis (e.g. results, interpretability, transparency)?
S – Stakeholders / Safety: Are there any risks if you would accept all suggestions without checking them? Who/What could be affected?

Question 2: Responsible checking and human oversight

Describe at least two checks you would perform yourself before accepting any changes to your script (e.g. running tests on a small dataset, checking R help pages, comparing to your original analysis plan).
Identify one suggestion from the AI that you would not implement (or would modify) and explain why.
How would you document which AI suggestions you accepted or rejected (e.g. comments in code)?

Question 3: Adjusting the code with human‑in‑the‑loop
Outline a short, practical plan (3–5 steps) for how you would proceed to adjust your code based on the AI’s feedback, while maintaining human oversight. For example, you might:

Select and rank suggestions (most useful / least disruptive first).
Implement only a subset of changes manually, step by step.
Re‑run the script on test data and compare outputs to your original results.
Add comments explaining why you changed certain parts and why you left others unchanged.



A BRAVE(R) prompt for step 2: annotating your improved R code
Select a part of the code you would like to adapt according to the recommendation of the AI tool. Craft a BRAVE(R) prompt that asks an AI coding tutor to help you annotate your improved R code. Use the template below and adapt it to your own script.
B – Boundaries: How long and detailed may the comments be?
R – Role: Which role should the AI take (e.g. “R coding tutor for social science researchers”)?
A – Audience: For whom are the comments written (e.g. “a researcher with basic R skills who needs to understand the workflow”)?
V – Variables: Which parts should be annotated (e.g. each major code chunk, data‑cleaning steps, model fitting, plotting)?
E – Expectations: What is the main goal (e.g. “add clear, correct comments so that another researcher can reproduce and understand my analysis”)?

title: Responsible GenAI for Coding in R
text:
In this exercise you will learn how to use an AI tool to assist you with writing code in R using the BRAVE(R) framework and keeping human oversight. This is in contrast with letting the AI tool write the enitire code from scratch (ghostwriting): the AI produces R code to build a chart, but you do not learn how it works, and you cannot tell whether it is right.
Instead you will proceed as follows:

Find reliable code from a trusted, curated source.
Understand it line by line, using AI as a tutor, not an author.
Adapt it to your own study design.
Verify the result (human oversight).

During the exercise, AI is a sparring partner that explains and suggests. You remain the author and the final reviewer. If you cannot evaluate the output, that is a signal that you need to understand the topic better before you rely on the tool (human oversight).

Data safety reminder. Never paste private, unpublished, participant, or otherwise sensitive data into an AI tool. That is why this exercise uses simulated data that you generate yourself. The simulation code is provided below.



By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

Locate trustworthy graphics code in the R Graph Gallery.
Read and annotate ggplot2 code so that every line has a comment in your own words.
Adapt a grouped boxplot from a 7 × 2 to a 4 × 3 study design.
Write prompts using the BRAVE(R) framework (Boundaries, Role, Audience, Variables, Expectations, Refine) to make Generative AI explain and refine code.
Apply human-oversight checks to confirm the boxplot matches the data.

title: Translating SPSS Syntax into R with the BRAVE(R) Framework
text:
Asking an AI tool to translate SPSS syntax can be tricky if you accept the output uncritically. The R code will usually look right and run without error, but might use a different default than SPSS (a different variance assumption, a different skewness formula, a different way of handling missing data). The numbers then disagree, and you have no idea why.
So in this exercise AI is a translator you supervise:

Give the AI a precise, well-scoped prompt using the BRAVE(R) framework.
Read the translation and identify where R’s defaults differ from SPSS.
Run the code on data you control and verify the results make sense.


Data safety reminder. Never paste real, unpublished, or participant data into a GenAI tool. This exercise uses simulated data you generate yourself, so nothing sensitive ever leaves your machine.




Write a BRAVE(R) prompt that asks AI to translate SPSS syntax into R.
Recognise common SPSS versus R default mismatches and check for them.
Run and verify an AI-produced translation against simulated data.
